name: Coulomb’s law
kicker: The force between two charges · Weakens with distance squared
briefing: Rub a balloon on your hair and it can lift the strands, because electric charges push and pull on each other. Coulomb’s law tells exactly how hard: the force grows with the sizes of the two charges and falls off with the square of the distance between them, so twice as far means one-fourth the force. French engineer Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured it in 1785 with a delicate twisting-wire instrument called a torsion balance.
answerHtml: Coulomb’s law (accept Coulomb’s inverse-square law; prompt on Coulomb, inverse-square law, or electrostatic force; do not accept “Gauss’s law,” “Ohm’s law,” or “Newton’s law of gravitation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henry Cavendish appears to have discovered this law in the 1770s, but his results stayed unpublished until James Clerk Maxwell edited his papers about a century later. In 1767, Joseph Priestley had guessed this law by analogy with gravity, reasoning from the fact that a charged hollow metal container exerts no electric force on objects inside it.
tossups.r: It was published by a French engineer in 1785. For 10 points, name this inverse-square law for the force between two electric charges.

tossups.p: This law’s discoverer also showed that the poles of magnets attract and repel with a force that weakens with the square of the distance. To establish this law in 1785, he measured how far a thin wire twisted in a torsion balance when two small charged balls pushed each other apart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the electric force between two charges equals k times the product of the charges divided by the distance squared.

tossups.p: The scientist who formulated this law also wrote a prize-winning study of friction, and the simple model of dry friction in which sliding friction does not depend on speed is often named for him. He spent years as a military engineer on the Caribbean island of Martinique.
tossups.r: The SI unit of charge is named for him. For 10 points, name this inverse-square law of electric force.

tossups.p: Ernest Rutherford’s formula for alpha particles bouncing off gold nuclei assumed this law, and its match with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden’s data supported the idea of a tiny, dense nucleus. In Niels Bohr’s model of hydrogen, this law gives the attraction that keeps the electron in orbit.
tossups.r: Like charges repel under it. For 10 points, name this law describing the electric force between two point charges.

tossups.p: Chemists use this law to explain why magnesium oxide, made of ions with charges of plus two and minus two, has a far higher melting point and lattice energy than sodium chloride. Because water weakens the force described by this law about 80 times compared with a vacuum, salt crystals can come apart into ions when they dissolve.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, which says the electric force between charges is proportional to the product of the charges.

tossups.p: The constant in this law, about 9 times 10 to the ninth in SI units, equals one divided by four pi times the permittivity of free space. That huge constant means two charges of one SI unit each, held one meter apart, would exert a force of about 9 billion newtons on each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law for the force between two point charges, written F equals k q one q two over r squared.

tossups.p: Between a proton and an electron, the force described by this law is roughly 10 to the 39th power times stronger than the gravitational pull between them. Unlike Newton’s law of universal gravitation, which it closely resembles, this law describes a force that can either attract or repel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inverse-square law of electrostatics, which says like charges repel and opposite charges attract.

tossups.p: According to this law, the positively charged protons packed into an atomic nucleus should push one another apart with enormous force; the strong nuclear force overcomes that push at very short range. In stars, protons must get past a barrier set by this law, with help from quantum tunneling, before they can fuse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the electric force between two charges falls off with the square of the distance.

tossups.p: Under this law, moving two charged objects twice as far apart cuts the force between them to one-fourth, while doubling both of their charges makes the force four times as strong. So doubling both charges and the distance at the same time leaves the force unchanged.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law for the force between electric charges, which has the same inverse-square form as Newton’s law of gravitation.

tossups.p: Applying Gauss’s law to a sphere drawn around a single point charge gives back this law, which is valid for charges at rest. When several charges are present, the principle of superposition says the total force on one charge is the vector sum of the forces this law gives for each of the others.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of electrostatics, which says the force between two charges is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

tossups.p: Dividing the force given by this law by the size of a small test charge gives the electric field around a point charge. The force in this law points along the straight line joining the two charges, and by Newton’s third law, each charge feels an equal and opposite push or pull.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, written F equals k q one q two over r squared.

tossups.p: Thirteen years before Henry Cavendish used a torsion balance to measure the density of Earth, a French physicist used a similar twisting-wire instrument to establish this law. This law has the same form as Newton’s law of gravitation, with electric charges taking the place of masses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance squared.

tossups.p: Chemists use this law to explain periodic trends: an outer electron that sits closer to a nucleus with a larger effective charge is pulled more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it. That is why ionization energy generally rises from left to right across a period.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, which says opposite charges attract with a force that grows as they get closer.

tossups.p: Photocopiers depend on the force described by this law, which pulls tiny charged toner particles onto oppositely charged areas of a drum. The same force lets electrostatic precipitators in smokestacks pull charged specks of ash out of the air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the electric force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges.

tossups.p: Outside a uniformly charged sphere, this law works as if all of the sphere’s charge were squeezed into a single point at its center, just as Isaac Newton showed for the gravity of a planet. Inside a charged hollow metal shell, the forces this law predicts from all parts of the shell cancel out.
tossups.r: Like charges repel under it, and opposite charges attract. For 10 points, name this inverse-square law for the force between electric charges.

trap.title: Which inverse-square law?
trap.body: Several laws show up in the same tossups. Coulomb’s law gives the force between two charges; Gauss’s law links the electric flux through a closed surface to the charge inside; Ohm’s law links voltage, current, and resistance. Newton’s law of universal gravitation has exactly the same inverse-square form, so “proportional to the product, inversely proportional to the distance squared” fits both until you hear whether the clue is about charges or masses.
trap.fix: Charges, k, “like charges repel,” torsion balances, and 1785 mean Coulomb’s law. Masses, G, and planets mean Newton’s law of gravitation; closed surfaces and flux mean Gauss’s law. Saying only “Coulomb” or “inverse-square law” earns a prompt, so be ready to say the whole name.
